blocks.text: 6S Home Reset is a guided home-transformation application that turns the 6S Success methodology into a room-by-room, zone-by-zone working system. It breaks a whole-home reset into 114 bounded micro zones across 20 room types, each engineered to finish in 15 to 90 minutes and end in a photographable, auditable change of state. In a single flow it acts as a work-session guide, a photographic evidence system, an AI coach that builds a plan from the household's own photos, and a sourced shopping companion, running on a professional standard operating procedure library rather than a generic checklist.

This document has two parts. Part I is the current-state specification for the validated v2.4 artifact: the single-file application already running and gate-tested as a Claude artifact. Part II is the committed scope for the production mobile product on the Apple App Store and Google Play, covering architecture, feature deltas, store compliance, monetization, and a phased engineering roadmap. It wins because it is the only home-organization product that pairs a complete professional SOP library with AI plans built from the user's own photos and three-way sourced product picks, delivered as a system a household can actually sustain.

Part III is new in this revision: an MVP Beta build plan grounded in a full code analysis of the v2.4 artifact. It defines the smallest shippable beta of the app, provisionally titled 6S Success Home Micro Zones: Organization & Housekeeping for the stores, that proves the core zone-reset loop on real homes. The code analysis confirmed every headline content count exactly and identified the two dependencies that must be replaced to leave the artifact host.

Part IV is added in this revision: the committed usability, data-collection, and visualization changes from a seven-discipline review of the running MVP (product, QA, front-end, back-end, marketing, customer success, and support). Its headline: the beta must instrument its own loop, show the before/after transformation, and turn AI on, or it will demo without learning.
What it is

6S Home Reset is a guided home-transformation application for families and individuals. It operationalizes the 6S Success methodology (Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain) at the micro-zone level: 114 bounded zones across 20 room types, each engineered to complete in 15 to 90 minutes and end in a photographable, auditable change of state. The app is simultaneously a work-session guide, a photographic evidence system, an AI coach, and a sourced shopping companion.
Current platform

A single-file React application (about 277 KB, roughly 4,300 lines including embedded datasets) executing as a Claude artifact. Persistence uses the artifact key-value storage API; AI vision features call the Anthropic Messages API through the artifact's built-in proxy. There is no external backend, no build system, and no third-party service dependency.
Who it serves
Primary: a household adult driving a home reset. Secondary: family members executing shared standards. The design assumes standards must survive children, tired Tuesdays, and 7:40 a.m.

blocks.text: The app's instructional content is not shipped as static copy. It is generated at runtime from one normalized source: a single field manual corpus, one product library, and per-room editorial, driven through three instruction engines. This keeps every zone's six activities maintainable in one place while producing the full body of guidance the user works through.
SOP dataset

Derived from the 6S Home Micro Zone SOP Field Manual (the Micro Zone Manual dataset), normalized once and stored in compact form (about 74 KB). The original 684-row activity corpus is not stored row by row: each zone carries its own identity and variables, and its six activity rows are regenerated at runtime from step templates. The result is content-identical to the manual at roughly one-seventh the size.

blocks.label: Reading the runner
blocks.text: The Zone Runner holds the core value loop: pick a zone, photograph the starting state, receive an AI Sort Plan, execute six guided steps with sub-procedures and one-tap sourcing, photograph the result, receive a scored Coach's Review, and close with the Sustain audit. The other five screens route users into and out of that loop.

Two AI capabilities anchor the core value loop: a Sort Plan built from the user's before photos, and a scored Coach Review of the after photos. Both call a single model with strict JSON-only prompting, so every response maps deterministically into the interface. Constrained schemas are also the compliance posture: coach output stays inside contracts the product controls rather than free-form generation.

blocks.text: Reliability layer
The AI path is wrapped in a reliability layer, every element of which was validated in harness.

items: Image shrink: photos are re-shrunk to 640 px before transport, cutting the image tokens each request sends versus the source photo.
Timeout: each request is bounded by a timeout so a hung call cannot stall the loop.
Retry: one automatic retry with backoff on failure.
Tolerant JSON extraction: parsing succeeds even when the model wraps the JSON in code fences, preambles, or postambles.
Truncation repair: if a reply is cut off, the parser backtracks to the last structurally complete value and recovers a usable object.
Errors are surfaced verbatim to the user rather than swallowed.

blocks.label: Validated in harness
blocks.text: The truncation-repair logic achieved 100 percent recovery in a sweep that truncated a reference reply at every third character. Combined with tolerant extraction, this means a partial or messily framed model response still yields a valid Sort Plan or Coach Review rather than a failed screen.

Two facilities carry all durable state: the artifact key-value storage API for structured data, and the same store for photos held as chunked JPEG data. Everything the user builds across sessions lives in the four keys below.

A single batched object keyed by roomId/zoneId: step booleans, substep bitmasks per step, done and audit timestamps, drift flag, photo id arrays (before and after), out-the-door tally, cached AI plan (plus its handled checklist), and review.

blocks.text: 5.2 Hardened photo pipeline

This pipeline was hardened against real storage failures encountered during development. It is the reference design for the mobile port's local layer, even though the port replaces the chunking mechanism with a file system.

rows: Capture / upload
Native camera (capture=environment) or library upload. Six photos per gallery per side.
Decode
createImageBitmap with an img fallback, a 40 MB guard, and explicit format-failure messaging.
Compress
Multi-pass quality-then-dimension step-down to a hard budget of about 175 KB, verified against 48 MP sources.
Save

A single write is attempted first. On rejection, a tiny self-test distinguishes 'too big' from 'storage down,' then chunk sizes are probed downward (96 to 48 to 16 to 6 KB), verified by read-back, with the working size cached. Every write retries with backoff.
Fallback
If storage refuses photos entirely, photos run session-only with an honest one-time notice. Galleries, AI analysis, and zone completion all continue unblocked.
Migration
Version 1 single-photo keys auto-migrate into version 2 galleries.

blocks.label: Proven under failure
blocks.text: The save path was proven in harness against simulated backends capped at 5 MB, 100 KB, 30 KB, and 10 KB, under transient rate-limiting, and fully broken. In every case the app degraded honestly rather than losing the user's work.

The app is continuous with the 6S Success book identity. A warm paper ground carries the interface, with a single terracotta accent for action and emphasis. Fraunces sets the display type over a Newsreader serif body, with a monospace utility face reserved for times, minute estimates, and codes.

The six step colors are the product's semantic spine. Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, and Sustain each own a fixed hue that recurs everywhere a step is represented, so a user learns the palette once and reads progress at a glance across every screen.

blocks.text: Rationale

items: Anchor to the value moment. The paywall sits at the 2-room wall, so price against the felt value of a fully guided home rather than per unlocked feature.

Follow category convention on annual plans. Lifestyle and home-organization subscriptions commonly offer annual billing. A recommended annual discount in the 40 to 50 percent range versus twelve monthly payments trades a lower headline price for committed retention and steadier AI cost forecasting.

Price Household as the retention upgrade, not a multiplier. Zone ownership across up to 5 members is the methodology's retention engine, so Household should be a modest step above single-user Plus, priced as "the family standard holds," not as five seats.

Bound the cost floor before locking anything. The free tier's 3-analysis cap and the fair-use cap on Plus limit AI cost of goods. Confirm the recommended Plus price clears blended AI cost per active subscriber with margin before committing.

blocks.label: How to validate
blocks.text: Test price sensitivity during beta with the 6S Success community as the recruit pool: run at least one alternative price band, add a short willingness-to-pay question at the 2-room wall, and watch Free-to-Plus conversion and the annual-versus-monthly mix before setting store prices.

6S Home Reset does not launch into a cold market. It launches into an ecosystem built alongside it and structured to feed it. The book teaches the method, the Micro Zone Manual is the source of the app's SOP dataset, the Product Library powers its Zone Kit, and the video series is a purpose-built acquisition engine. The strategic point is that these are not four separate marketing efforts. They are one funnel whose shape is set by a single fact: the content and the app share the same skeleton, the 114 micro zones.
The one-to-one funnel geometry

The video series is planned as 114 headless YouTube episodes plus 684 Shorts. That count is not arbitrary. The app has 114 micro zones, and the six-S sequence run across all of them accounts for 684 distinct activities, exactly the number of Shorts. The series therefore maps one-to-one onto the product. Each long episode is the reset of one zone. Each Short is one activity within a zone, for example resetting a single junk drawer or wiping down one glass surface.

Because of that alignment, every piece of content has a precise destination inside the app. A Short about resetting a drawer is not generic inspiration; it is a direct funnel to the exact app screen for that drawer. The link in the video description deep-links to that zone, so the viewer arrives already knowing what they are about to do and finds the professional plan for it waiting. The content generates demand and the app fulfills it, for the same task and at the same level of granularity.

Top of funnel: the book and manual as credibility

The book "6S Success: Home Edition" and the Micro Zone Manual sit at the top of the funnel and do a different job than the video. They are not per-zone hooks; they are proof that the method is real, complete, and seriously authored. The book explains why the six S's work in order, Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, and Sustain, and the manual shows the depth behind a single zone. That credibility converts a skeptical viewer into someone willing to install, and it gives the brand a reason to exist beyond an app icon.

blocks.text: The free-to-paid boundary is a belief boundary

The freemium line is drawn where conviction is highest, not where cost is highest. The free tier gives away the entire methodology, the Entryway plus one room the user picks, and three AI analyses. That is enough to finish a real zone and see the scored, photographed result. The upgrade to 6S Plus is asked for at the two-room wall, after the product has already proven itself, which is why the plan frames the finished zone as the pitch. As the risk register notes, the program's full length can intimidate, so onboarding sells one short zone at a time and the "Next up" recommendation rather than the full twenty-room program.
Organic surfaces: the before/after share card

The before/after share card is both a feature and a distribution channel. Each card pairs the before-and-after diptych with the zone name, the time spent, and the count of items released. When a user shares it, they broadcast a specific, credible transformation to people who share their context, which is the top of a new funnel that costs nothing to run. The items-released count doubles as the motivational north-star stat inside the app and the hook on the card, so the same number that keeps one user engaged helps recruit the next.

blocks.label: Why the funnel compounds
blocks.text: The video series is a fixed-cost asset that keeps working after it ships. Because each piece points at a durable zone screen rather than a dated promotion, the back catalog of Shorts becomes a standing acquisition surface, and user-generated share cards extend it without further production spend.

6S Home Reset competes in the home organization, cleaning, and decluttering app category, alongside general-purpose checklist and habit trackers that users bend toward the same goal. The category is real and populated, but it is fragmented by function. Each incumbent solves one slice of the problem well and leaves the rest to the user's own discipline. The opening is that no widely used app in this space ships a complete professional method. They ship containers, schedules, or inventories that the user must fill with expertise they do not have.

It is that they occupy adjacent slots. A schedule tells you a room is due. An inventory tells you what is in it. A checklist tells you a task exists. None of them tells a tired adult standing in front of a cluttered drawer what professional sequence to run, what the drawer should look like when finished, or what to buy to hold the result.
How 6S Home Reset differs
The difference is categorical, not incremental. 6S Home Reset is a system, not a checklist. Three capabilities combine to make that claim real, and no incumbent ships all three:

items: A complete professional SOP library. Every one of the 114 zones carries authored, expert-cued instructions for all six steps, expanded into checkable procedure sub-steps that encode real technique, for example dwell-time chemistry before wiping in wet zones, degrease before sanitize at cooking surfaces, and child-height sweeps in kids' spaces. This is know-how, not a to-do list.

AI plans built from the user's own photos. The Sort Plan reads up to two before photos of the actual space and returns a tailored verdict on what belongs and what to relocate, donate, discard, or keep, plus visible hazards, and the Coach Review scores the after photos against the target state. The guidance is grounded in the user's real space, not a generic template.

Three-way sourced product recommendations. The Zone Kit resolves the exact products a zone needs and offers three sourced picks per product, a top name brand, a best generic, and a best overall, each with a real retail listing and a direct link, surfaced at the moment of need.

blocks.label: The checklist trap
blocks.text: A checklist assumes the user already knows how to do each item. That assumption is why home-organization attempts stall. The professional SOP closes the expertise gap the incumbents leave open, which is the difference between a list that reminds you to clean the fridge and a system that tells you to watch for thermal shock while you do it.
The durable moat

Differentiation only matters if it is hard to copy. Any competitor can bolt an AI feature onto a schedule or a checklist, and some will. What they cannot cheaply reproduce is the depth of authored assets underneath, built over the course of this project and kept current on a fixed cadence. The moat is three compounding assets:

items: The authored SOP corpus. The zone-by-zone manual behind the app, spanning 114 micro zones across 20 rooms, the per-zone expert cues, and the branching sub-step engine represent a large body of domain authoring. This is the asset a well-funded competitor would have to sit down and write from scratch, zone by zone and surface by surface, and the one an AI cannot convincingly fake, because it is specific professional technique.

The sourced product catalog. The Product Library of 97 standards, 1,812 zone-product mappings, and 291 retail picks, maintained on a 90-day sourcing refresh, is both a user-value asset and the affiliate revenue engine. Keeping it accurate is ongoing labor that deepens the moat each quarter rather than letting it decay.

The content funnel. The one-to-one mapping of 114 episodes and 684 Shorts onto the app's zones and activities is a proprietary acquisition machine a competitor cannot replicate without first building an equivalently structured product and then producing the matching content library against it.

blocks.label: Honest read on defensibility
blocks.text: The individual features are copyable in isolation; the combination and the corpus behind it are not. An incumbent could add photo-based AI in a quarter. Reproducing an authored, zone-by-zone professional SOP, plus a maintained three-way sourced catalog, plus a one-to-one content funnel is a multi-year program, and by the time a competitor finished, the catalog refresh cadence and the growing back catalog of share cards and Shorts would have moved further ahead.

blocks.label: Positioning line to defend
blocks.text: Hold the line stated in the product definition: the only home-organization app that combines a complete professional SOP library, AI plans built from your actual photos, and three-way sourced product recommendations. It is a system, not a checklist. Every competitive conversation should return to the assets the category cannot match, not to feature parity on any single one.

The release product is a local-first mobile application backed by a thin managed backend. The device holds the full experience and runs offline; the backend exists only for the capabilities an artifact cannot provide: accounts, sync, durable photo storage, AI proxying, and payments. blocks.text: Ownership and row-level security

The governing rule is household tenancy. Every record that a household creates carries a household_id, and row-level security restricts reads and writes to members of that household. A member's identity comes from the auth provider (Apple, Google, or email) and is resolved to a member row, which anchors every household-scoped query.

Zone ownership is the retention mechanism made concrete. The Sustain step's named owner becomes owner_member_id on zone_progress, constrained to a member of the same household, and audit-due notifications are addressed to that member. Reference data (zone, product, catalog_version) is globally readable but immutable to clients, so the 90-day sourcing refresh ships as a new catalog_version without an app update. Sensitive and financial records are write-protected from clients entirely: photos are reached only via signed URLs and removed on account deletion, subscription rows are written solely by the receipt-validation function, and ai_usage is written solely by the metered AI proxy.

Accessibility is treated as both a store expectation and a product value. Apple and Google both weight accessibility in review and in featuring decisions, and the audience for a home-reset system includes people managing physical limits, low vision, and fatigue. The commitment for v1.0 is that a full zone loop, from picking a zone through the Coach's Review, can be completed with a screen reader, at large text sizes, and without depending on color to carry meaning.
Screen readers

Every interactive element ships with an explicit VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) label and role, not a label inferred from an icon. The load-bearing controls are the step spine, checkable substeps, input chips, the I own this toggle, the before/after galleries, and the camera and upload actions. Progress is announced meaningfully, for example "Shine, 4 of 7 substeps done," rather than as a bare percentage, and photo thumbnails carry descriptive labels ("before photo 2 of 6") instead of a filename.
Scalable text

The interface honors Dynamic Type on iOS and the system font scale on Android across the full supported range. The Georgia-family serif display, system-sans body, and monospace utility type all scale, and layouts reflow rather than clip or truncate. The 560 px single-column shell is verified to remain usable at the largest accessibility text sizes, including the mission card, product sheet, and substep lists.
Color and contrast

The six step colors are the product's semantic spine, so meaning must never rest on them alone. Each step also carries its name, an icon, and its position in the sequence, and status is conveyed with text and shape, not just hue. Text and essential controls meet WCAG AA contrast against the warm paper ground, and the design is verified against common color-vision deficiencies so the Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain progression stays legible without color perception.
Touch targets and motion

Interactive targets, especially the dense substep checkboxes and input chips, meet the platform minimum tap size (roughly 44 pt on iOS, 48 dp on Android) with adequate spacing, so a reset can be run one-handed or with limited dexterity. The app respects the Reduce Motion setting: progress-ring fills, step-spine transitions, and share-card animations degrade to instant or simple state changes when motion is reduced.
Captions

Any onboarding or zone-loop video, including the optional App Store preview and any in-app clips drawn from the 6S Micro Zone Reset series, ships with accurate captions and does not rely on audio alone to convey instructions.

blocks.label: Value, not just compliance
blocks.text: The same choices that pass accessibility review, clear labels, legible type at any size, and meaning carried by more than color, make the product easier for everyone to run on a tired weekday morning. Accessibility and the everyday-usability goal are the same work.

blocks.label: Verification
blocks.text: Accessibility is a build gate, not a final polish pass. A screen-reader run of one complete zone loop and a largest-text-size layout check are added to the phased roadmap's exit criteria, alongside the existing engine and pipeline gates.

v1.0 ships US-first by deliberate choice. The methodology, engines, and datasets are language-neutral in structure, but two layers are bound to a market: the retail catalog and the units of measure. The plan below separates what must be true at US launch from what a later market expansion adds, so international readiness is designed for rather than retrofitted.
Retailers and catalog

The Product Library and its 291 retail picks are sourced across Amazon, Walmart, Target, Home Depot, and Lowe's, all US retailers, and the affiliate programs behind the monetization plan (Amazon Associates, Walmart Creator, Target Partners, and the Home Depot and Lowe's networks) are US storefronts. Because the catalog is served live from the backend with version stamps, a market's catalog can be swapped without an app release. International retailer coverage, which storefronts, which affiliate programs, and how sourcing quality is maintained per market, is an open item to resolve before any non-US launch.
Units

The source Micro Zone Manual is authored in metric, while the US launch audience thinks in imperial. The app should support both and let the user choose, with a sensible default from device locale. Measurements that surface in guidance and product sheets (quantities, sizes, container and bin dimensions) render in the selected system. This is a v1.0 capability because it serves the US audience directly, not only future markets.
Language

v1.0 ships in English. The interface, the step templates, and the AI JSON contracts should be built with strings externalized so that translation is a content task rather than a rewrite. AI-generated coach and Sort-plan output would need per-language prompting and review, which is scoped with, and gated behind, a specific target market rather than done speculatively.
Phased expansion

A recommended, illustrative sequencing to validate against real demand: English-language, imperial-friendly markets with strong Amazon presence first (for example Canada, the UK, and Australia), because they reuse the most catalog and language work; then priority non-English markets, each of which requires a localized catalog, translated content, and reviewed AI output. Each phase is gated on retailer and affiliate coverage being resolved for that market, not on a calendar.

blocks.text: Posture

The sensitive asset is photos of the inside of people's homes. The design position is that photos are private by default, encrypted in transit and at rest, never used for training, never shared without an explicit share action, and deleted with the account. AI analysis is user-initiated per photo set, so nothing is scanned passively.

blocks.label: Posture as positioning
blocks.text: This privacy posture is a marketing asset, not just a compliance obligation. The stance of never training on user photos and honoring deletion end to end is something to publish, not hide.
Children

The app is operated by adults. Kids' rooms are content, not users. There are no child accounts in v1.0, which keeps the product out of COPPA scope. In-app guidance nudges users to avoid uploading photos with identifiable children.
Chemical safety

Cleaning guidance includes incompatibility warnings, already built into the substep engine, for example chlorine and ammonia. Product safety notes surface from the catalog, and a general follow-product-labels disclaimer sits in the Terms and on the product sheet. This maps to the fourth S, Safety, in the Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain sequence.

blocks.label: Privacy stance
blocks.text: Analytics is privacy-respecting by design. There is no cross-app or cross-site tracking and no advertising identifier, so App Tracking Transparency is not triggered and should stay that way. Events are keyed to the user's own account, never to a device graph or third-party profile. No photo, home or room name, or user-typed text ever leaves the device in an analytics payload; events carry counts, phases, and enum properties only. This matches the private-by-default posture: photos are never used for training and never shared without an explicit action, and the same restraint governs what we measure.

blocks.text: Break-even sketch

items: A free user who never converts is bounded on cost. The hard 3-analysis free cap sets a worst-case AI COGS in the illustrative range of a few cents to about ten cents over their lifetime, plus negligible hosting. That user reaches break-even only through affiliate taps.

A converting user covers their own AI and hosting cost quickly. At an illustrative low-single-digit-cents COGS per analysis and a fair-use cap on Plus, even heavy AI use stays well under one month of net subscription revenue.

The portfolio view is what matters. Using the source's illustrative 5 percent Free-to-Plus conversion target at the 2-room wall, net subscription revenue from converters plus affiliate revenue across all activated users must cover the capped AI COGS of the non-converting majority. Because the free AI cost is hard-capped and metered from day one, that spread is bounded and controllable.

Sensitivity: the model is most sensitive to the confirmed store commission (15 versus 30 percent materially changes subscription net) and to the confirmed per-analysis AI price. Both must be locked before any pricing is set.

blocks.text: These two pieces of work turn the artifact into an app. They are the critical path; nothing else in the beta can be tested until they land.
1. Persistence, off the artifact host

items: Keep the existing storage interface (the get, set, delete wrappers and the save-photo call) so the screens do not change.
Back it with device storage: structured data (home, progress, owned gear) in SQLite or a key-value store, and photos written to the file system as files, with the record holding only a file URI.
Delete the chunking, size-probing, and session-only fallback layer. Native storage has no artifact quota, so that entire subsystem retires.
Collapse the current split (photo ids in progress, data-urls in local state, session photos in memory) into a single photo record with a URI. This removes the app's most fragile code.

blocks.text: 2. AI, through a thin server proxy

items: Stand up a small backend endpoint that holds the API key and forwards the Sort Plan and Coach Review calls. The app calls the proxy, never the model directly. No key ships in the binary.
Use an API configuration that is zero-retention and not used for training, and document it. This is both a compliance gate and a marketing asset.
Meter per user or per device so a free beta cannot run up unbounded cost (a hard cap on analyses per tester is enough for the beta).
Confirm the current model and raise the token cap at build time; keep the JSON contracts and the tolerant parser, which port as-is.
Keep AI optional: the app already works with AI disabled, so if the proxy is down the loop still completes on the static plan.

blocks.text: Seven disciplines reviewed the running MVP prototype and this spec: product management, software quality assurance, front-end, back-end, marketing, customer success, and support. They produced 59 findings against three themes the product owner asked to improve: usability, data collection, and visualization. This part turns the convergent findings into committed spec changes.

blocks.label: The five things every discipline circled
blocks.text: 1) The beta emits zero analytics events, so its own test questions are unanswerable. 2) The before/after transformation, the whole payoff, is captured but never shown to the user. 3) AI is unreachable by testers (endpoint off by default), so the differentiator and its attach rate go untested. 4) Every failure dies in a 3.4-second toast with nothing captured. 5) There is no in-app help, feedback, or diagnostic path, and home photos mean testers cannot even screenshot a bug.

None of these are deep rebuilds. They are the difference between a beta that demos and a beta that learns. The sections below are organized by the three themes; a prioritized do-next list closes the part.
Changes that make the app clearer, more motivating, and safer to use, drawn from the panel and ranked by severity.

rows: Guide first-run to one fast-win zone

First-run drops the tester into a 37-zone program instead of steering to a single finished zone. Onboarding should pick one high-payoff zone and walk it end to end so value lands in the first sitting.
High
Gate completion on a before AND an after photo
A zone can currently be marked done with only an after photo, which breaks the activation definition. Require one of each.
High
Show the before/after reveal on completion

The transformation is stored but never shown paired. On completion, present a before/after compare plus the items-released count and a Start-next-zone button. This is the conversion hinge from one zone to the next.
High
Make AI reachable, or show an honest off-state

AI is gated behind a manual endpoint no tester will set, so the flagship feature reads as a dead button. Ship the beta with the proxy pre-configured, and when no endpoint exists render an explicit off-state rather than an actionable dead-end.
High
Replace toast-only failures with persistent, recoverable error states
AI, photo decode, and storage all fail into a 3.4-second toast (AI with a silent 60-second wait, no cancel, no retry). Add persistent failure states with Retry and Cancel, and honest copy.
High
Add in-app help, feedback, and a photo-free diagnostic export
There is no way to report a problem in-app, and because the asset is home photos, testers cannot safely screenshot a bug. Add a Report-a-problem path and a redacted diagnostic export.
High
Add a top-level error boundary and clamp AI JSON before render
A render throw white-screens with nothing logged; an out-of-range AI score renders as 7/5. Add a recovery boundary and validate AI values (1 to 5, default arrays).
Medium
Fix the honest-storage notice and the in-memory fallback message
When photos run in memory the app still promises Stays on this device. Show the true state.
Medium
Accessibility pass
Status is carried by color alone, icon controls are unlabeled, and there is no dynamic-type or contrast provision. Add labels, non-color status, larger tap targets, and scalable text.
Medium
Clarify substep affordance
Checkable substeps look required but do not gate step completion. Make the affordance read as optional guidance, or gate on them, but not the ambiguous middle.
Medium

The beta must answer whether a household reaches a finished zone with before and after photos and then keeps going. Today it captures none of that. Everything below inherits the existing privacy contract: counts, enums, small integers, and booleans only; no photo, home name, room name, free text, or full endpoint URL ever enters telemetry.
Beta instrumentation, on device

Implement the loop-milestone events in the beta build itself, append-only and privacy-safe, rather than deferring them to the backend. This makes activation, AI attach, and step drop-off computable from a tester's device from day one.

blocks.text: Schema and pipeline changes

items: Store an append-only per-zone audit log (timestamp, result) instead of a single overwritten drift flag, so Sustain retention and the two-consecutive-drift redesign rule are computable
Capture the Sustain owner, reset trigger, and chosen cadence (weekly or monthly), and drive the audit-due banner off the chosen cadence rather than a hardcoded 7 days
Stamp the catalog version on device and on relevant events so sourcing refreshes are traceable
The AI proxy meters and logs per device or user (request count, latency, token cost, model), and pins the model server-side rather than trusting the client
A small on-device event client with an offline queue and a batched, PII-free flush to a privacy-respecting analytics store
Redaction rule: the AI endpoint URL may carry a token, so diagnostics and telemetry record at most its hostname, never the path or query

blocks.text: Two audiences: the user, who needs to feel momentum and see the change; and the team, who need discipline dashboards to run the beta. The prototype has the four signature user visualizations (progress rings, the six-segment step spine, zone-dot strips, stat tiles) but no completion reveal and no team views at all.
User-facing

items: The before/after compare on zone completion: the single most motivating view in a habit product, and it is currently absent
Items released as a hero stat, defined consistently with the metric and the future share card (donate plus discard)
A home-level momentum view (zones finished, streak, time this week) richer than the current three tiles, since keeping is the point
An honest time visualization based on measured minutes, replacing the budget-derived estimate

blocks.label: One shared foundation
blocks.text: All five dashboards read from the same two event families over the same aggregation layer. Build the pipeline once (Data Collection above); each discipline gets a view, not a separate integration. Every view is aggregate-only, with no per-household drill-down, so team data stays private.
The review reconciled the spec against the running build and against itself.

rows: Items released definition
Pin to donate plus discard only; relocate is tracked separately as items_relocated. The Part III code-analysis note had this backwards; the build actually over-counts by including relocate.
AI automatic retry
Part I describes one automatic retry with backoff. The ported prototype does a single attempt with no retry. Treat retry as a build-time requirement not yet present, and reconcile the two.
Time invested
The dashboard stat is the static budget prorated by steps done, not measured time. Relabel as estimated or, preferably, back it with real elapsed minutes (session_minutes).
Error boundary and AI JSON validation
Promote both from aspirational notes to explicit Acceptance Criteria gates: a top-level error boundary must exist, and AI values must be clamped before render.
Completion definition
Align the code with the Activation metric: a zone requires at least one before and one after photo to count as complete.

blocks.label: The one-line takeaway
blocks.text: The MVP proves the loop. To make the beta prove the business, instrument the loop, show the transformation, and turn AI on. Everything else is a refinement of those three.

A review of the book's chapter packages surfaced a plan change that strengthens this product's story. The book 6S Success: Home Edition is now a 50-chapter volume: Part 9 (Room-by-Room Playbooks) expanded from 10 to 20 chapters, one per room in the Micro Zone Manual (Ch 31 Entryway through Ch 50 Patio or Deck). Chapter 31, The Entryway, is written as the proof of a new applied format.

blocks.label: The funnel just got a second 1:1 rail
blocks.text: The app's rooms, the 114-video series, and now the book's Part 9 chapters all map one-to-one onto the same 20 rooms and their micro-zones. A reader finishing the book's Entryway chapter, a viewer watching an Entryway Short, and a user opening the app's Entryway are looking at the same five zones. Every piece of the ecosystem points at the same door.
What the app adopted from the Ch 31 canon

items: Room-as-zones framing: the room screen now states the zone count with 'do one, then the next, until the room is done', matching the book's rule that you 6S one zone at a time, never a whole room.

The call that matters here: each zone now surfaces its one genuinely hard decision (the paper with no verdict, the coat counted by weather, the tired mat), the element the book says earns a playbook its keep. Sourced from the Micro Zone Manual and merged into the app dataset.

The after photo as the standard: the completion reveal now states that the after photo is the zone's standard, aligning with the book's before-and-after room signature and the ideal-state photo (Ch 25).
Kit by job, types not brands: the app's per-step product chips already follow this; the book's per-room kit sections and the new Complete Product List appendix are the shared source.
